claims.source: Upon activation, mast-cell LynA is not rapidly degraded, and SFK-mediated signaling is amplified relative to macrophages.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing enhanced Erk phosphorylation in mast cells compared to macrophages.

claims.claim: Cell-specific c-Cbl expression builds cell specificity into the LynA checkpoint.
claims.source: Cell-specific c-Cbl expression thus builds cell specificity into the LynA checkpoint.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from macrophages and mast cells showing differential c-Cbl expression and LynA regulation.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) by Src-family kinases (SFKs) is the first enzymatic step in the activation of an innate immune response during a pathogen encounter.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) by Src-family kinases (SFKs) is the first enzymatic step in the activation of an innate immune response during a pathogen encounter.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ITAM signaling pathways.

claims.claim: Initiation of cell-activating signaling typically occurs within clusters of ITAM-coupled receptors such as FcγR or the hemi-ITAM Dectin-1.
claims.source: Initiation of cell-activating signaling typically occurs within clusters of ITAM-coupled receptors such as FcγR (Guilliams et al., 2014) or the hemi-ITAM Dectin-1 (Brown, 2006; Deng et al., 2015), nucleated by highly multivalent immunoglobulin-G-decorated pathogens or fungal cell-wall β-glucans, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: SFKs and phosphorylated ITAMs trigger activation of the tyrosine kinase Syk.
claims.source: Together, SFKs and phosphorylated ITAMs trigger activation of the tyrosine kinase Syk (Lowell, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The SFKs and Syk drive activation of membrane-proximal signaling through adaptor proteins, cytoskeleton-modulating proteins, and Tec kinases.
claims.source: The SFKs and Syk then drive activation of membrane-proximal signaling through adaptor proteins; cytoskeleton-modulating proteins, such as the FAK/Pyk2 kinases and Paxillin; and Tec kinases, which activate second-messenger pathways via phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and phospholipases Cγ (PLCγ1/2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Early ITAM signaling events ultimately lead to downstream signaling through Erk1/2 and other pathways.
claims.source: These early events ultimately lead to downstream signaling through Erk1/2 and other pathways (Lowell, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The responsiveness of innate immune cells is tightly regulated.
claims.source: As the byproducts of activated macrophages can be toxic (e.g. release of reactive oxygen species) and drive inflammation (e.g. release of tumor necrosis factor α), the responsiveness of innate immune cells is tightly regulated (Goodridge et al., 2011; Takai, 2002; Sondermann, 2016; Chiffoleau, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by phosphatases CD45 and CD148.
claims.source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion contribute to tuning the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells.
claims.source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) and inhibitory ITAMs contributes to tuning the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells.
claims.source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases contributes to tuning the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells.
claims.source: Multiple mechanisms work together to tune the responsiveness of macrophages and other myeloid cells, including negative regulation by the phosphatases CD45 and CD148 (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Bakalar et al., 2018), cytoskeletal barriers to diffusion (Jaumouillé et al., 2014), signaling via immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) (Abram and Lowell, 2008) and inhibitory ITAMs (Hamerman and Lanier, 2006; Hamerman et al., 2009), and degradation and sequestration of signaling molecules targeted for polyubiquitination by ubiquitin ligases (Lutz-Nicoladoni et al., 2015; Liyasova et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In myeloid cells, SFKs typically include Fgr, Fyn, two isoforms of Hck, and two splice forms of Lyn.
claims.source: The SFKs, which in myeloid cells typically include Fgr, Fyn, two isoforms of Hck, and two splice forms of Lyn, may also have positive and negative functions (Abram and Lowell, 2008; Mkaddem et al., 2017; Alvarez-Errico et al., 2010; Scapini et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: SFKs may have positive and negative functions in myeloid cells.
claims.source: The SFKs, which in myeloid cells typically include Fgr, Fyn, two isoforms of Hck, and two splice forms of Lyn, may also have positive and negative functions (Abram and Lowell, 2008; Mkaddem et al., 2017; Alvarez-Errico et al., 2010; Scapini et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Activated LynA is rapidly and specifically targeted for polyubiquitination and degradation, forming the basis of a signaling checkpoint that blocks spurious macrophage activation.
claims.source: Layered onto the traditional positive- and negative-regulatory roles of the SFKs, activated LynA (the longer of the two Lyn splice forms) is rapidly and specifically targeted for polyubiquitination and degradation, forming the basis of a signaling checkpoint that blocks spurious macrophage activation (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: The LynA checkpoint can be bypassed when LynA is upregulated, with LynA acting as a rheostat to tune macrophage sensitivity.
claims.source: This checkpoint can be bypassed when LynA is upregulated, with LynA acting as a rheostat to tune macrophage sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: LynA is transcriptionally upregulated when macrophages are treated with interferon (IFN)-γ.
claims.source: For instance, LynA is transcriptionally upregulated when macrophages are treated with interferon (IFN)-γ, and these primed cells have a lower threshold for SFK-mediated signaling (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: IFN-γ-primed macrophages have a lower threshold for SFK-mediated signaling.
claims.source: For instance, LynA is transcriptionally upregulated when macrophages are treated with interferon (IFN)-γ, and these primed cells have a lower threshold for SFK-mediated signaling (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The molecular mechanism that selectively targets LynA for polyubiquitination has not been elucidated previously.
claims.source: The molecular mechanism that selectively targets LynA for polyubiquitination has not been elucidated previously.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work.

claims.claim: Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors.
claims.source: Unlike Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages, which are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Freedman et al., 2015), mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation; small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in the context of a cell-particle interaction (Andrews et al., 2009; Felce et al., 2018; Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation.
claims.source: Unlike Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages, which are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Freedman et al., 2015), mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation; small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in the context of a cell-particle interaction (Andrews et al., 2009; Felce et al., 2018; Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in mast cells in the context of a cell-particle interaction.
claims.source: Unlike Dectin-1 and FcγR signaling pathways in macrophages, which are typically triggered in the context of pathogen-induced µm-scale clusters of receptors (Goodridge et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2016; Freedman et al., 2015), mast-cell FcεR signaling has a low threshold for activation; small or even monovalent antigen-IgE complexes can induce a signaling response in the context of a cell-particle interaction (Andrews et al., 2009; Felce et al., 2018; Carroll-Portillo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The binding dynamics of Syk with FcεRI in mast cells is unaffected by the size of receptor aggregates.
claims.source: Supporting this more permissive signaling function, the binding dynamics of Syk with FcεRI in mast cells is unaffected by the size of receptor aggregates (Schwartz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Mast cells express LynA.
claims.source: Like macrophages, mast cells express LynA, and the disparity in the receptor sensitivity of these two cell types has not previously been explained.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of fact about mast cell protein expression.

claims.claim: The disparity in the receptor sensitivity of macrophages and mast cells has not previously been explained.
claims.source: Like macrophages, mast cells express LynA, and the disparity in the receptor sensitivity of these two cell types has not previously been explained.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work.

claims.claim: 3-IB-PP1 specifically inhibits a variant of the SFK-inhibitory kinase Csk (CskAS).
claims.source: To reveal the requirements for LynA degradation, we synchronized receptor-independent SFK activation using the designer inhibitor 3-IB-PP1 (Okuzumi et al., 2010; Okuzumi et al., 2009; Schoenborn et al., 2011), which specifically inhibits a variant of the SFK-inhibitory kinase Csk (CskAS) (Freedman et al., 2015; Schoenborn et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Csk is responsible for phosphorylating a key inhibitory tyrosine in the C-terminal tail of all the SFKs.
claims.source: Csk is responsible for phosphorylating a key inhibitory tyrosine in the C-terminal tail of all the SFKs.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Csk function.

claims.claim: Inhibiting CskAS with 3-IB-PP1 disrupts the dynamic equilibrium between Csk and the phosphatases CD45 and CD148, leading to rapid and robust SFK activation.
claims.source: Inhibiting CskAS with 3-IB-PP1 disrupts the dynamic equilibrium between Csk and the phosphatases CD45 and CD148, which dephosphorylate the inhibitory tyrosine, leading to rapid and robust SFK activation (Chow and Veillette, 1995; Zhu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the phosphorylation and likely activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl.
claims.source: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the phosphorylation and likely activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl (Feshchenko et al., 1998; Dou et al., 2012; Freedman et al., 2015) and the preferential polyubiquitination and degradation of LynA in macrophages (Freedman et al., 2015), but it was not clear whether these two events were linked.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the preferential polyubiquitination and degradation of LynA in macrophages.
claims.source: 3-IB-PP1-induced SFK activation leads to the phosphorylation and likely activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase c-Cbl (Feshchenko et al., 1998; Dou et al., 2012; Freedman et al., 2015) and the preferential polyubiquitination and degradation of LynA in macrophages (Freedman et al., 2015), but it was not clear whether these two events were linked.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: c-Cbl mediates rapid degradation of LynA upon activation in macrophages.
claims.source: Using knockout and overexpression models coupled with analyses of protein abundance and cell signaling, we now demonstrate that c-Cbl controls the steady-state expression of LynA and mediates its rapid degradation upon activation in macrophages.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from c-Cbl knockout experiments showing impaired LynA degradation.

claims.claim: LynA is targeted by c-Cbl in response to phosphorylation of tyrosine 32 (Y32) within the LynA unique region.
claims.source: Quantitative targeted mass spectrometry shows that LynA is targeted by c-Cbl in response to phosphorylation of tyrosine 32 (Y32) within the LynA unique region, a process mediated by LynA, LynB or the shorter isoform of Hck.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing Y32 phosphorylation and mutagenesis data showing Y32 is required for degradation.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of LynA Y32 is mediated by LynA, LynB or the shorter isoform of Hck.
claims.source: Quantitative targeted mass spectrometry shows that LynA is targeted by c-Cbl in response to phosphorylation of tyrosine 32 (Y32) within the LynA unique region, a process mediated by LynA, LynB or the shorter isoform of Hck.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cotransfection experiments showing which SFKs can induce LynA degradation in trans.

claims.claim: The c-Cbl recognition mode for LynA via Y32 is distinct from the slower-phase action of c-Cbl and other E3 ligases on LynB and the other SFKs.
claims.source: This recognition mode is distinct from the slower-phase action of c-Cbl and other E3 ligases on LynB and the other SFKs (Freedman et al., 2015; Sanjay et al., 2001; Sanjay et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing differential degradation kinetics and by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The LynA checkpoint is cell-specific.
claims.source: Finally, we have discovered that the LynA checkpoint is cell-specific.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from macrophages and mast cells.

claims.claim: Mast cells express very little c-Cbl but abundant Cbl-b.
claims.source: In mast cells, which express very little c-Cbl but abundant Cbl-b, LynA is not rapidly degraded upon activation, a function that can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data comparing c-Cbl and Cbl-b levels in mast cells and macrophages.

claims.claim: Rapid degradation of LynA in mast cells can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl.
claims.source: In mast cells, which express very little c-Cbl but abundant Cbl-b, LynA is not rapidly degraded upon activation, a function that can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by saRNA experiments showing that increasing c-Cbl expression in mast cells induces LynA degradation.

claims.claim: The differential regulation of c-Cbl and LynA may drive mast cells toward a lower activation threshold than macrophages.
claims.source: The differential regulation of c-Cbl and LynA may drive mast cells toward a lower activation threshold than macrophages.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing differential c-Cbl expression and LynA stability in mast cells versus macrophages.

claims.claim: Knockout of c-Cbl profoundly impaired the degradation of activated LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
claims.source: Knockout of c-Cbl profoundly impaired the degradation of activated LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment, with LynA levels remaining at 100% after 1 min of exposure to 3-IB-PP1 in CskASc-CblKO BMDMs compared to 60% in CskAS BMDMs (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by densitometry quantification of immunoblots shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: CskASc-CblKO BMDMs expressed 3-fold more LynA protein than CskAS at steady state.
claims.source: CskASc-CblKO BMDMs also expressed 3-fold more LynA protein than CskAS at steady state (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by densitometry quantification of immunoblots shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Cbl-b does not have a role in suppressing the steady-state level or promoting the activation-induced degradation of LynA.
claims.source: Although it has been reported previously that c-Cbl and Cbl-b have some redundant functions (Naramura et al., 2002; Purev et al., 2009), we were unable to detect any role for Cbl-b in suppressing the steady-state level or promoting the activation-induced degradation of LynA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from Cbl-b knockout experiments showing no effect on LynA degradation.

claims.claim: Upon treatment for 1 min with 3-IB-PP1, LynA was 81% reduced in CskASCbl-bKO compared to 60% in CskAS BMDMs.
claims.source: Upon treatment for 1 min with 3-IB-PP1, LynA was 81% reduced in CskASCbl-bKO compared to 60% in CskAS BMDMs (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by densitometry quantification of immunoblots shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs show a compensatory upregulation of c-Cbl protein expression.
claims.source: This increase in LynA degradation may be explained by a compensatory upregulation of c-Cbl protein expression in CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Syk phosphorylation is enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs.
claims.source: Notably, Syk phosphorylation is enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs, consistent with the higher expression level and longer half-life of LynA protein (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Syk phosphorylation is enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, likely due to the direct role of Cbl-b on Syk inhibition.
claims.source: Syk phosphorylation is also enhanced in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, but this is likely due to the direct role of Cbl-b on Syk inhibition (Sohn et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data and citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Erk phosphorylation in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs is impaired, likely due to the loss of the adaptor function of c-Cbl in PI3K signaling.
claims.source: Erk phosphorylation in 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASc-CblKO BMDMs is impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), likely due to the loss of the adaptor function of c-Cbl in PI3K signaling (Ueno et al., 1998; Hunter et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, Erk1/2 phosphorylation is enhanced, likely due to the negative-regulatory role of Cbl-b for Syk and other upstream signaling intermediates.
claims.source: In 3-IB-PP1-treated CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs, Erk1/2 phosphorylation, like Syk phosphorylation, is enhanced, again likely due to the negative-regulatory role of Cbl-b for Syk and other upstream signaling intermediates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data and inference from known Cbl-b functions.

claims.claim: siRNA knockdown of c-Cbl resulted in modest but specific knockdown (70% reduced).
claims.source: Immunoblots of siRNA-transfected BMDM lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showed modest but specific knockdown of c-Cbl (70% reduced) and Cbl-b (60% reduced), importantly, without a corresponding increase in c-Cbl expression as a consequence of Cbl-b knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: siRNA knockdown of Cbl-b resulted in modest but specific knockdown (60% reduced).
claims.source: Immunoblots of siRNA-transfected BMDM lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showed modest but specific knockdown of c-Cbl (70% reduced) and Cbl-b (60% reduced), importantly, without a corresponding increase in c-Cbl expression as a consequence of Cbl-b knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in impaired degradation of LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment in siRNA experiments.
claims.source: As in the knockout models, loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in impaired degradation of LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment and increased steady-state expression of LynA protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in increased steady-state expression of LynA protein in siRNA experiments.
claims.source: As in the knockout models, loss of c-Cbl but not Cbl-b resulted in impaired degradation of LynA in the first few minutes of 3-IB-PP1 treatment and increased steady-state expression of LynA protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Without c-Cbl upregulation in Cbl-b-knockdown BMDMs, there was no increase in the LynA degradation efficiency or decrease in the steady-state level of LynA protein.
claims.source: Without c-Cbl upregulation in Cbl-b-knockdown BMDMs, there was no increase in the LynA degradation efficiency or decrease in the steady-state level of LynA protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D), supporting our hypothesis that this observation in CskASCbl-bKO BMDMs was c-Cbl-dependent.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from siRNA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: c-Cbl is solely responsible for the rapid and specific degradation of LynA.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that c-Cbl is solely responsible for the rapid and specific degradation of LynA, whereas other E3 ubiquitin ligases can complement the canonical SFK-binding and -polyubiquitinating function of c-Cbl (Sanjay et al., 2001; Sanjay et al., 2006), which mediates slower degradation of LynA and the other SFKs (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from knockout and siRNA experiments and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Other E3 ubiquitin ligases can complement the canonical SFK-binding and -polyubiquitinating function of c-Cbl, which mediates slower degradation of LynA and the other SFKs.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that c-Cbl is solely responsible for the rapid and specific degradation of LynA, whereas other E3 ubiquitin ligases can complement the canonical SFK-binding and -polyubiquitinating function of c-Cbl (Sanjay et al., 2001; Sanjay et al., 2006), which mediates slower degradation of LynA and the other SFKs (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and inference from the data.

claims.claim: Macrophage Hck, Fgr, and LynB are degraded >10 fold more slowly than LynA during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
claims.source: Susceptibility to rapid, activation-induced degradation differentiates LynA from the splice variant LynB and the other abundant SFKs in macrophages, Hck (59 and 56 kDa transcripts) and Fgr (Scapini et al., 2009), which are degraded >10 fold more slowly than LynA during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Fyn has been reported to play an important role in macrophage inflammatory signaling.
claims.source: The SFK FynT (Fyn) has also been reported to play an important role in macrophage inflammatory signaling (Mkaddem et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Macrophage Fyn is long-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
claims.source: We now confirm that, like Hck, Fgr, and LynB, macrophage Fyn is long-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 2A), although we have been unable to detect Fyn activation in response to 3-IB-PP1 (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Fyn activation in response to 3-IB-PP1 in macrophages was not detected.
claims.source: We now confirm that, like Hck, Fgr, and LynB, macrophage Fyn is long-lived during 3-IB-PP1 treatment (Figure 2A), although we have been unable to detect Fyn activation in response to 3-IB-PP1 (Freedman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: LynA is rapidly degraded in Jurkat cells treated with 3-IB-PP1, in contrast to longer-lived Lck and Fyn.
claims.source: As in macrophages, LynA is rapidly degraded in Jurkat cells treated with 3-IB-PP1, in contrast to longer-lived Lck (Schoenborn et al., 2011) and Fyn (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2B and citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Cell types that do not express Lyn may lack an analogous, rapid off-switch for SFK signaling.
claims.source: This highlights the unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation and suggests that cell types, such as T cells, that do not express Lyn may lack an analogous, rapid off-switch for SFK signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing unique LynA degradation properties.

claims.claim: c-Cbl overexpression in Jurkat cells increased the rate of LynA degradation.
claims.source: As predicted, c-Cbl overexpression in Jurkat cells increased the rate of LynA degradation (30% depletion after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1 in c-Cbl-overexpressing Jurkat cells versus no detectable depletion in either ctrl or Cbl-b-overexpressing cells) (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Jurkat cells, which do not normally express Lyn, are capable of supporting rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation of LynA.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with the knockout and siRNA experiments in BMDMs, demonstrating that Jurkat cells, which do not normally express Lyn, are capable of supporting rapid, c-Cbl-mediated degradation of LynA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from Jurkat cell transfection experiments.

claims.claim: LynB lacks a 21 amino-acid insert found in the unique region of LynA.
claims.source: LynB, which lacks a 21 amino-acid insert found in the unique region of LynA (Figure 3D), was less efficiently degraded (10% depleted after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1) than LynA (40% depleted after 5 min) in c-Cbl- and memCskAS-cotransfected Jurkat cells (Figure 3E–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3D and citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: LynB was less efficiently degraded (10% depleted after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1) than LynA (40% depleted after 5 min) in c-Cbl- and memCskAS-cotransfected Jurkat cells.
claims.source: LynB, which lacks a 21 amino-acid insert found in the unique region of LynA (Figure 3D), was less efficiently degraded (10% depleted after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1) than LynA (40% depleted after 5 min) in c-Cbl- and memCskAS-cotransfected Jurkat cells (Figure 3E–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid degradation is preserved in the Jurkat model.
claims.source: Again, these data mirror our findings in CskAS BMDMs (Freedman et al., 2015) and confirm that the unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid degradation is preserved in the Jurkat model.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from Jurkat cell experiments and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The unique-region insert of LynA (residues 23–43) contains a tyrosine residue reported to be phosphorylated in cancer cells (Y32).
claims.source: We hypothesized that the c-Cbl recognition site in LynA must lie within the unique-region insert (residues 23–43), absent in LynB (Yi et al., 1991; Stanley et al., 1991), which contains a tyrosine residue reported to be phosphorylated in cancer cells (Y32; Huang et al., 2013; Tornillo et al., 2018), a predicted threonine phosphorylation site (T27; NetPhos 3.1, Blom et al., 2004) and a predicted lysine ubiquitination site (K40; UbPred, Radivojac et al., 2010) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Substituting tyrosine 32 with either alanine or phenylalanine blocked the rapid degradation of LynA.
claims.source: Substituting tyrosine 32 with either alanine or phenylalanine blocked the rapid degradation of LynA (Figure 3E), reducing the depletion after 5 min treatment with 3-IB-PP1 from 40% (LynA) to 10% (LynAY32A) or 8% (LynAY32F), levels indistinguishable from LynB (10%) (Figure 3E–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Substitution of Y32 did not alter the membrane localization of a unique-region construct at steady state or after 3-IB-PP1 treatment.

results.result: c-Cbl, but not Cbl-b, is solely responsible for the rapid degradation of LynA in macrophages. Knockout of c-Cbl profoundly impaired LynA degradation (100% remaining at 1 min vs 60% in controls) and increased steady-state LynA expression 3-fold. Cbl-b knockout showed no impairment of LynA degradation, though compensatory c-Cbl upregulation was observed. siRNA knockdown experiments confirmed these findings without compensatory effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C63 are well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (knockout mice, siRNA knockdown) showing c-Cbl specifically mediates rapid LynA degradation. The data include quantitative immunoblot analysis with appropriate controls and statistical testing. The compensatory upregulation observation (C52) is appropriately qualified as inference. The distinction between rapid c-Cbl-mediated degradation and slower degradation by other E3 ligases is supported by kinetic data and citations.

results.result: Tyrosine 32 (Y32) in the unique region of LynA is required for its rapid degradation by c-Cbl. Substitution of Y32 with alanine or phenylalanine blocked rapid degradation (reducing depletion from 40% to 10% or 8% after 5 min), without affecting membrane localization. Other predicted sites (K40R, T27A) did not affect degradation. Y32 mutants showed 2-3 fold higher steady-state expression than wild-type LynA.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C81 are strongly supported by systematic mutagenesis experiments in Jurkat cells showing Y32 is necessary for rapid degradation. The data include quantitative time-course measurements with appropriate controls (LynB, other mutations). Microscopy data (C77) confirms Y32 mutation doesn't affect localization, ruling out an indirect effect. The correlation between degradation kinetics and steady-state expression strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: LynA Y32 is phosphorylated in response to SFK activation in primary macrophages. Quantitative LC-MS/MS showed pY32 was 6-12 fold enriched in nonubiquitinated LynA from 3-IB-PP1-treated BMDMs versus resting cells. Phosphorylated Y32 was 6.0-6.4 fold higher in polyubiquitinated versus nonubiquitinated LynA, suggesting pY32 is a prerequisite for rapid polyubiquitination by c-Cbl.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 are supported by rigorous quantitative mass spectrometry with isotope-labeled internal standards and appropriate controls. The experimental design (using CskASCbl+/- mice and 15s pulse treatment) was optimized to detect transient phosphorylation. Two independent biological replicates showed consistent results. The inference that pY32 precedes polyubiquitination (C90) is reasonable given the enrichment in polyubiquitinated species, though the temporal relationship is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: SFKs themselves, rather than downstream kinases (Syk, FAK/Pyk2) or T-cell SFKs (Lck, Fyn), induce LynA degradation. LynA degradation was unaffected by Syk or FAK/Pyk2 inhibition but abrogated by SFK inhibition. Only catalytically competent LynA was degraded in JCaM1.6 cells; kinase-dead mutants (T410K, Y397F, K275R) were resistant. Activated Lck could not induce LynA degradation in trans.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 are supported by systematic pharmacological inhibitor studies and kinase-dead mutant experiments. The inhibitor experiments include appropriate controls showing pathway-specific effects (pErk, pPaxillin). The use of multiple kinase-dead mutants (C95, C97) affecting different aspects of catalytic activity strengthens the conclusion. The Lck experiment (C96) provides a negative control showing kinase activity alone is insufficient.

results.result: LynA degradation can be induced in trans by specific SFKs. Wild-type LynA, LynAY32A, LynB, and Hck56 (but not Hck59) induced degradation of catalytically-impaired LynAT410K by 20-40% after 5 min. Fgr and Lck could phosphorylate Zap70 and c-Cbl but could not induce LynA degradation, while Hck59 and FynB could only phosphorylate the LynA activation loop. Lyn appears most efficient at inducing degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C109 are supported by extensive cotransfection experiments testing multiple SFKs. The experimental design using catalytically-impaired LynAT410K as substrate is appropriate for detecting trans effects. The data reveal substrate specificity patterns, though the interpretation involves some inference (C103, C107, C109). The conclusion that Lyn is most efficient (C109) is appropriately qualified as potentially due to kinetics or efficiency differences. Expression level differences are acknowledged as a confounding factor.

results.result: The LynA checkpoint is cell-specific: mast cells express very little c-Cbl (20% of macrophage levels) but abundant Cbl-b (80% of macrophage levels). Consequently, mast cell LynA is not rapidly degraded upon activation and shows 30% higher steady-state expression than rested macrophages. This results in 3-4x more LynA protein and stronger Erk phosphorylation in mast cells versus macrophages during 3-IB-PP1 treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C121 are supported by comparative analysis of mast cells and macrophages using immunoblotting, RNAseq data from ImmGen, and flow cytometry validation of mast cell identity. The quantitative differences in c-Cbl expression, LynA stability, and signaling output are well-documented. The inference that differential c-Cbl expression tunes cell responsiveness (C120, C121) is reasonable given the convergent data, though it remains correlative rather than directly causal in this dataset.

results.result: Rapid degradation of LynA in mast cells can be rescued by induced overexpression of c-Cbl. Transfection of c-Cbl-targeting saRNA increased c-Cbl expression 2-fold, leading to 30% LynA degradation after 15 min 3-IB-PP1 treatment (versus undetectable degradation in controls) and complete suppression of Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C125 are supported by saRNA experiments showing gain-of-function rescue of LynA degradation in mast cells. The 2-fold increase in c-Cbl is modest but sufficient to induce measurable effects on both LynA stability and downstream signaling. The complete suppression of Erk phosphorylation (C125) is striking and supports functional significance. However, n=3 for these experiments is relatively small, and the saRNA approach may have off-target effects not fully controlled for.

results.result: LynA is uniquely susceptible to rapid degradation compared to other SFKs. Macrophage Hck, Fgr, LynB, and Fyn are degraded >10 fold more slowly than LynA during 3-IB-PP1 treatment. In Jurkat cells, LynA is rapidly degraded while Lck and Fyn are longer-lived. This suggests cell types lacking Lyn may lack an analogous rapid off-switch for SFK signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 are supported by comparative degradation kinetics in both macrophages and Jurkat cells. The >10 fold difference (C64) is cited from prior work. The speculation about cells lacking Lyn (C69) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion. The data clearly establish LynA's unique degradation properties among SFKs, though the functional implications for T cells remain speculative.

results.result: c-Cbl overexpression in Jurkat cells increases LynA degradation rate (30% depletion after 5 min versus no detectable depletion in controls). LynB, lacking the 21 amino-acid unique region insert, is less efficiently degraded (10% vs 40% for LynA after 5 min). The unique susceptibility of LynA to rapid degradation is preserved in the Jurkat model.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by transfection experiments in Jurkat cells showing c-Cbl dose-dependence and the importance of the unique region. The comparison with LynB (C72-C73) provides a natural control differing only in the unique region. The data validate that the degradation mechanism operates in a heterologous system, supporting generalizability. However, transient transfection creates cell-to-cell variability in expression levels.

results.result: Background and context claims establishing the role of SFKs in ITAM signaling, mechanisms of myeloid cell regulation, the LynA checkpoint from prior work, and the 3-IB-PP1 experimental system. These claims provide the scientific foundation and rationale for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C38 are primarily background knowledge and citations to prior literature, including the authors' previous work. These are appropriately cited and represent established knowledge in the field. The novelty statement (C27, C33) correctly identifies gaps addressed by the current work. The description of the 3-IB-PP1 system (C34-C38) is well-supported by citations.

results.result: Summary claims stating the main findings: c-Cbl targets LynA via phosphorylated Y32, this depresses steady-state LynA expression in macrophages, the mechanism is distinct from slower degradation of other SFKs, and differential c-Cbl expression builds cell specificity into the LynA checkpoint, potentially driving different activation thresholds in mast cells versus macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C126 are high-level summary statements that integrate findings from multiple experiments. These are well-supported by the collective data presented in the manuscript. The mechanistic claims (C4, C5, C43) are directly demonstrated. The functional implications (C10, C47, C126) involve reasonable inference from the data but remain somewhat speculative regarding physiological significance, as the experiments use artificial activation (3-IB-PP1) rather than physiological stimuli.

results.result: The unique region of LynA contains Y32, previously reported to be phosphorylated in cancer cells, along with predicted phosphorylation and ubiquitination sites at T27 and K40.
results.evaluation: Claims C75 and C82 are supported by citations to prior literature and computational predictions. These provide context for the mutagenesis experiments. The prior reports of Y32 phosphorylation in cancer cells (C82) support the biological relevance of this site, though its function in hematopoietic cells was previously unclear.

results.result: Syk and FAK are phosphorylated on activating tyrosine residues in CskAS BMDMs treated with 3-IB-PP1, as previously reported.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by citation to the authors' prior work. This establishes that the 3-IB-PP1 system activates expected downstream signaling pathways, validating the experimental approach.

results.result: Lyn is a key regulator of mast-cell ITAM signaling. CskAS mast cells were validated as homogeneous for mast cell markers FcεR1α and c-Kit by flow cytometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are supported by citation to prior literature (C113) and flow cytometry data (C114). The validation of mast cell identity is important for interpreting the comparative experiments with macrophages.
